--- title: "13 — Tracking a drifting DARM parameter" description: "The DARM loop's calibration parameters drift, forcing continuous re-measurement. Inject a known slow variation into an actuation strength and recover κ(t) with a Lataire–Pintelon basis fit on leakage-free P&S snapshots — within an honest Cramér–Rao band, with the drift's resolvability proven by a computed bound." image: thumbnails/13.svg categories: [calibration, closed-loop, DARM, time-varying] freeze: true --- ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## What you'll learn - Why a *drifting* plant is a system-ID problem, not a re-measurement chore. - Recovering a time-varying parameter **κ(t)** from leakage-free snapshots, with a real CRB. - Proving the drift is **resolvable** with a computed bound — not eyeballing the plot. ::: The [DARM calibration page](08-darm-calibration.qmd) recovers the loop's sensing, actuation, and response at **one instant**. But the reason DARM calibration is the slowest recurring LIGO measurement is that those parameters **drift** — the optical gain, the coupled-cavity pole, and the actuation strengths wander over minutes to hours, so the calibration is re-measured again and again. This page treats that drift head-on: as a slowly time-varying system to *identify*, not a nuisance to average away. ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} ## Round 1 — the sysID, not the physics This is the first, deliberately narrow step: a **known, simple** drift (a smooth deterministic profile) injected into one actuation strength, real sensing pole, no optical spring. The goal is only to show the machinery **tracks a drifting parameter within its error bar**. A physically faithful drift (a stochastic/GP wander, the SRC-detuning optical spring that carries the DARM pole from real to complex, several parameters at once) is a later round. Rendered with `freeze: true`. ::: ::: {#322c8a26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Setup — import the presentation glue"} import sys, pathlib _p = pathlib.Path.cwd() for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]: if (_c / "docs" / "darm_tv_demo.py").exists() and str(_c / "docs") not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c / "docs")) if (_c / "darm_tv_demo.py").exists() and str(_c) not in sys.path: sys.path.insert(0, str(_c)) import numpy as np import darm_tv_demo as dd from IPython.display import display ``` ::: ## The idea: locally stationary snapshots The plant drifts far more slowly than one measurement record (an hour-scale drift versus a ~16 s record), so within any single record it is **locally stationary** — the Pintelon–Schoukens picture of a linear model around a slowly-moving operating point. That licenses a two-step estimator: 1. **Snapshot.** At a sequence of times, take one leakage-free periodic-multisine measurement and recover the instantaneous actuation strength with **Pcal as the ruler**. Because the sensing `C` cancels in the stage-to-Pcal ratio, each snapshot is *immune to sensing drift* and carries an honest per-estimate σ. 2. **Basis fit.** Fit `κ(t) = Σ cₖ bₖ(t)` in a time-basis (Legendre) to the snapshot series by weighted least squares — a Lataire–Pintelon basis expansion in two-step form. The coefficient covariance **is** the Cramér–Rao bound on the drift curve κ(t) and its rate. We drift the **ESD (TST) stage** — the one whose strength really wanders in an interferometer, as charge builds on the reaction mass — with a 5 %, hour-scale profile. ::: {#8e652c1c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Run the campaign — snapshot the drift, fit κ(t)"} c = dd.campaign(seed=777) ``` ::: ## Tracking the drift The injected truth, the per-record snapshots with their error bars, and the recovered κ(t) with its CRB band: ::: {#cecf2714 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="κ(t): injected truth, snapshots ± σ, LP fit ± CRB"} dd.drift_fig(c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The fit rides straight through the snapshots and follows the injected drift — a 5 % excursion resolved cleanly, even though each single snapshot only pins κ to about a percent. ## Is the recovery honest? A curve through points is easy; a curve that knows its own uncertainty is the point. The recovery residual (recovered − truth) stays inside the ±σ Cramér–Rao band — the error bar neither collapses (which would be fabricated confidence) nor balloons (which would be uselessly conservative): ::: {#85272e6d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Tracking error vs the CRB band"} dd.tracking_error_fig(c) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## The feasibility gate: is the drift resolvable? Before calling a drift "trackable" or "buried in noise," compute the bound. The tracking σ from the fit is far below the injected drift amplitude, so the drift is genuinely **resolved**, not noise — and the local-stationarity approximation costs a fraction of a percent, well under the per-snapshot error: ::: {#d3e23be3 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Resolvability — a computed bound, not an eyeball"} display(dd.resolvability_table(c)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown} **Feasibility gate — the injected drift is resolvable (a computed bound, not an eyeball)** | feasibility quantity | value | note | | --- | --- | --- | | injected drift amplitude | 0.0040 | 5% of κ | | per-snapshot σ_κ (median) | 0.0008 | 1.01% of κ | | tracking σ_κ (LP fit, median) | 0.0003 | 0.42% of κ | | resolve ratio = amp / tracking σ | 12× | ≫ 1 ⇒ drift resolved, not noise | | local-stationarity error | 0.22% | record ÷ drift timescale — the approximation cost | ::: ::: The resolve ratio is a knob, not a limit: more periods per snapshot, more snapshots, or a stronger drive all buy it down further — the same Fisher levers as everywhere else in the pipeline. ## Honest gaps The drift here is a *known, deterministic* profile on a *single* scalar with the sensing pole held real. It does not yet include a stochastic (GP) wander, the SRC-detuning optical spring that turns the DARM pole complex, several parameters drifting at once, or the one-shot (rather than two-step) Lataire–Pintelon fit. Those are the next rounds. What this page establishes is the foundation they build on: the machinery **tracks a time-varying parameter within a Cramér–Rao bound**, and the "can we track it?" question gets a numeric answer — see `notes/darm-calibration-via-pns.md`.
